summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys the Slavs: the etymology of the word "Slav" and the Slavic autonym, early Slavic migrations into Byzantine borders and the Balkans, and the assimilation of non-Slavic peoples. It also covers the modern division into West, East and South Slavs, the Pan-Slavism movement, and Slavic minority populations in former Soviet and Warsaw Pact states.
one_line: Overview of the Slavs, covering the origin of their name, early migrations, modern subgroups, Pan-Slavism, and Slavic diaspora populations.
key_facts: The English word Slav may derive from Middle English sclave, borrowed from Medieval Latin sclavus or slavus and Byzantine Greek σκλάβος sklábos "slave".
The Byzantine term Sklavinoi was loaned into Arabic as Saqaliba by medieval Arab historiographers.
Around the 6th century, Slavs appeared on Byzantine borders in great numbers, and by the end of the 6th century had settled the Eastern Alps regions.

Present-day Slavs are classified into West Slavic (chiefly Poles, Czechs and Slovaks), East Slavic (chiefly Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians), and South Slavic (chiefly Serbs, Bulgarians, Croats, Bosniaks, Macedonians, Slovenes, and Montenegrins).
The word "Slavs" was used in the national anthem of the Slovak Republic (1939–1945), Yugoslavia (1943–1992) and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (1992–2003).
Stephen J. Lee estimates that by the end of World War II in 1945, the Russian population was about 90 million fewer than it could have been otherwise.

No archaeological evidence of a Slavic settlement in the Balkans could be securely dated before c. 600 AD, though Slavic raids across the lower Danube may be dated to the first half of the 6th century.
Menander Protector mentions a Daurentius (577–579) who slew an Avar envoy of Khagan Bayan I.
The Slavic autonym is reconstructed in Proto-Slavic as *Slověninъ, plural *Slověne.
In the 6th century, Procopius wrote in Byzantine Greek of the Sklaboi and related forms, while his contemporary Jordanes referred to the Sclaveni in Latin.
In the postulated homeland region (present-day Ukraine), Slavs had contacts with the Iranic Sarmatians and the Germanic Goths.
Dalmatian Romance was spoken until the high Middle Ages before its speakers were eventually assimilated into the Slavs.
Roman Jakobson considered the autonym a derivation from slovo "word", originally denoting people who speak the same language.

Pan-Slavism, which came into prominence in the mid-19th century, emphasized the common heritage and unity of all Slavic peoples and was used as a political tool by the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union.
Kazakhstan has the largest Slavic minority population among former Soviet states, with most being Russians.

entities.name: Slavs
entities.role: the subject people, divided into West, East and South Slavs and described in this note

entities.name: Procopius
entities.role: 6th-century writer in Byzantine Greek who referred to the Sklaboi and related forms

entities.name: Jordanes
entities.role: contemporary of Procopius who referred to the Sclaveni in Latin

entities.name: Menander Protector
entities.role: historian who mentions a Daurentius (577–579) who slew an Avar envoy of Khagan Bayan I

entities.name: Stephen J. Lee
entities.role: historian who estimates the Russian population was about 90 million fewer by the end of World War II in 1945

entities.name: Roman Jakobson
entities.role: scholar who considers the Slavic autonym a derivation from slovo "word"

entities.name: Lozinski
entities.role: scholar who argues *slava originally meant worshipper

entities.name: S.B. Bernstein
entities.role: scholar who speculates the autonym derives from a reconstructed Proto-Indo-European *(s)lawos

entities.name: Henrich Bartek
entities.role: scholar (1907–1986) who argued the Old East Slavic Slavuta for the Dnieper River derives from slova and is the origin of Slovene

entities.name: Daurentius
entities.role: Slavic figure (577–579) who slew an Avar envoy of Khagan Bayan I, per Menander Protector

entities.name: Khagan Bayan I
entities.role: Avar ruler whose envoy was slain by Daurentius

entities.name: Pan-Slavism
entities.role: movement emphasizing common heritage and unity of Slavic peoples, prominent from the mid-19th century

entities.name: Yugoslavia
entities.role: political union covering most South Slavs, which broke apart in the 1990s

entities.name: Soviet Union
entities.role: state that used Pan-Slavism as a political tool and held hegemonic influence over most Slavic-majority nations until 1989–1991

entities.name: Russian Empire
entities.role: empire that used Pan-Slavism as an ideology justifying territorial conquests in Central Europe

entities.name: Warsaw Pact
entities.role: Eastern bloc alliance within which Soviet propaganda used Pan-Slavism after World War II

entities.name: Kazakhstan
entities.role: country with the largest Slavic minority population, mostly Russians

entities.name: Byzantine Empire
entities.role: empire that ruled the South Slavs for centuries and whose records describe Slavic arrivals

entities.name: Ottoman Empire
entities.role: empire that ruled the South Slavs for centuries in the Balkans

entities.name: Austria-Hungary
entities.role: empire that ruled the South Slavs for centuries

entities.name: Venice
entities.role: power that ruled the South Slavs for centuries

entities.name: Sarmatians
entities.role: Iranic people with whom Slavs had contacts in the postulated homeland

entities.name: Goths
entities.role: Germanic people with whom Slavs had contacts in the postulated homeland

entities.name: Illyrians
entities.role: Paleo-Balkan people assimilated by Slavs; the modern Albanian nation claims descent from them
